description: We are two enthusiastic engineering students eager to turn academic knowledge into tangible innovation through out-of-school projects. Combining Aerospace Engineering—with a passion for space and aeronautics—and Computer, Telecommunications, and Electronic Engineering—focused on remote sensing and data analysis—we bring complementary skills to build new solutions, gain hands-on experience, and grow as future engineers.
summary: Our project builds an open-source tool that combines Earth, Moon, and Mars datasets from space agencies to find and describe new terrestrial analogs for future lunar and Martian bases and landing sites. Instead of relying only on well-known sites like Atacama or Haughton Crater, we scan deserts, polar regions, volcanic fields, arid terrain, and caves worldwide. Each candidate is scored on temperature, dust, biology, terrain morphology, and geology. The analyses run in Python notebooks and produce comparative charts and world maps that make results easy to inspect and reuse. We chose to build an application rather than a static report because users need to explore interactively, compare sites, and incorporate new data as it becomes available. Keeping data, scoring methods, and maps in one place ensures the work stays reproducible and can grow over time. It is designed to be user-friendly and accessible, allowing researchers, students, and mission planners to explore analog landscapes from a shared evidence base. By turning scattered agency data into clear, map-based insight, the project helps to compare analog sites and support landing-site studies. Its main purpose is practical:  to make the search for terrestrial analogs of the Moon and Mars open and usable by a wide range of people. Looking ahead, the next generation of researchers will need exactly this kind of shared knowledge to turn distant landscapes into reachable destinations.
details:
Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars

Project's name: E.L.M.A. (Earth-based Lunar & Martian Analogues)

1) What the project does

The project delivers an open-source application that integrates Earth, Moon, and Mars datasets from NASA and other space agencies to identify, score, and map new terrestrial analogs for future lunar and Martian bases and landing sites. Rather than revisiting the same handful of well-known sites (Atacama, Haughton Crater, McMurdo Dry Valleys), the tool scans the entire globe across deserts, polar regions, volcanic fields, arid terrains, and caves, and ranks each candidate through a transparent, multi-parametric scoring system.

The project was developed as a series of separate Python scripts, each dedicated to a specific physical or environmental dimension. Every script produces its own charts, heat maps, and world maps, and the results were then assembled into a single application that brings together all the collected data into a composite ranking, supporting site comparison and mission planning.

2) How it works — Section by section

2.1 Parameters considered

Across the modular analyses, the project evaluated a consistent set of physical, environmental, and geological parameters to characterize each candidate analog site. These parameters were selected to reflect the conditions that most directly affect equipment performance, human survivability, and mission planning on the Moon and Mars.

  • Thermal parameters: mean surface temperature, diurnal temperature range, seasonal temperature range, absolute minimum and maximum temperatures, subsurface thermal diffusivity, skin depth (diurnal and seasonal), and depth of thermal stabilization.
  • Atmospheric and wind parameters: atmospheric pressure, wind speed (mean, maximum, gust), dynamic pressure, dust optical depth (τ), and seasonal dust storm timing (solar longitude Ls).
  • Radiation parameters: galactic cosmic ray (GCR) dose rate, solar energetic particle (SEP) exposure, ultraviolet (UV) irradiance, and natural background radiation levels at terrestrial sites.
  • Geochemical and resource parameters: perchlorate concentration in soil, water ice availability and stability, water activity, soil composition (basaltic, anorthositic, saline, etc.), and presence of hydrated minerals.
  • Geomorphological parameters: terrain morphology (crater, lava tube, rille, dune field, polar desert), surface roughness, slope, regolith thickness, and presence of caves or subsurface voids.
  • Biological parameters: soil organic content, microbial habitability, toxicity (heavy metals, perchlorates), and potential for bioremediation (mycorrhizae, biochar).
  • Operational and logistical parameters: site accessibility, isolation level, energy storage requirements (day–night cycle length), and availability of continuous solar illumination.

Each parameter was normalized and scored on a 0–100 scale, with higher values indicating closer similarity to the lunar or Martian reference condition. The weights assigned to each parameter in the composite index are documented in the code and can be adjusted by the user to reflect different mission priorities.

2.2 Data acquisition layer

The foundation of the project is the collection of open datasets from multiple sources. The NASA POWER API provided daily meteorological data (T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, WS2M) for any point on Earth without requiring authentication. The Planetary Data System (PDS) Geosciences Node supplied lunar temperature data from the LRO Diviner instrument. Mars reference values were drawn from NASA Fact Sheets, REMS/Curiosity, InSight HP³, and MSL/RAD. For geological and geomorphological parameters, we referenced published literature and datasets from NASA, ESA, and peer-reviewed studies. All values are documented in code comments and metadata so results can be verified or extended.

2.3 Surface temperature module

This module compares the diurnal and seasonal temperature ranges of Earth, Moon, and Mars. Using NASA POWER daily data, each terrestrial grid point was reduced to four metrics: mean daily range, maximum daily range, seasonal range, and absolute extremes. These were compared against lunar reference values (≈293 K diurnal range at the equator) and Martian values (≈60 K diurnal range from REMS). The module computes a similarity percentage and a stress index. Graphs used: heat maps of global temperature ranges, bar charts comparing lunar/Martian targets with terrestrial sites, and a scatter plot of mean temperature versus diurnal range with the planetary target highlighted as a reference star.

2.4 Subsurface thermal module

The subsurface module models heat propagation using the standard exponential attenuation of temperature amplitude with depth: ΔT(z) = ΔT_surf · exp(−z/δ), where δ is the thermal skin depth. For Earth, lunar, and Martian soils we applied published thermal diffusivity values and estimated the depth at which diurnal and seasonal oscillations fall below 5% of the surface value. This revealed a key insight: the lunar regolith stabilizes thermally within 1.5–2 m, Martian regolith within ~4 m, and terrestrial soils require 10–15 m. Graphs used: log-log plots of amplitude versus depth, three-panel vertical profiles (depth on the y-axis, temperature on the x-axis), and bar charts comparing stabilization depths across the three bodies.

2.5 Martian wind and dust module

The Mars wind module synthesized published data from the NASA Ames GCM, REMS, TWINS, and the 20-year dust devil catalog. It computed dynamic pressure (q = ½ρv²) to demonstrate that Martian winds, although fast, exert about 60 times less force than equivalent terrestrial winds because of the low atmospheric density. Dust optical depth was modeled as a function of solar longitude (Ls), with the storm season between Ls 185° and 310°. Graphs used: dual-axis seasonal cycle plots, bar charts comparing terrestrial and Martian wind speeds, dynamic pressure curves, and polar-projection maps of dust optical depth across the Martian surface.

2.6 Multi-parameter analog finder

Five additional parameters were analyzed in independent modules: radiation (GCR dose), water and ice availability, day–night cycle and energy storage, biological viability (regolith toxicity, bioremediation potential), and dust/micrometeorite exposure. For each parameter, a shortlist of candidate terrestrial sites was compiled from the literature and scored qualitatively. Graphs used: radar charts for the top three sites, horizontal bar charts of individual parameter scores, and a combined map locating every candidate site.

2.7 Geological analog module

Inspired by the geological sections of the Astronomical Langrenus website, this module mapped five lunar geological features—basaltic maria, anorthositic highlands, impact craters, rilles and lava tubes, and regolith—to specific terrestrial analogs. Each analog was scored for how faithfully it reproduces the lunar feature. Graphs used: a heat map matrix crossing lunar features with terrestrial sites, a world map color-coded by feature type, and a bar chart of analog scores.

2.8 Discovery of new analog sites

To avoid simply reusing NASA's classic training sites, we built a dedicated module that evaluates emerging candidates such as the Bodelé Depression (Chad), Owens Valley (California), the dried Aral Sea bed, Alpachaca (Peru), Capelinhos (Azores), Jingpo Lake (China), Kauhako Crater (Hawaii), and Rummu Quarry (Estonia). Each site receives scores for temperature, dust, biology, morphology, and geology, which are combined into a weighted composite index. Graphs used: a parameter heat map, a horizontal bar chart of the composite score, and a Robinson world map with ranked annotations.

2.9 Martian analog finder

A dedicated module identifies terrestrial analogs of Mars using eight parameters: mean temperature, diurnal range, atmospheric pressure, gravity, solar irradiance, GCR dose, dust, and water availability. Candidate sites were drawn from Atacama, McMurdo, Devon Island, MDRS Utah, HI-SEAS, Rio Tinto, Ramsar, Svalbard, Puna Plateau, and southern Morocco. Score functions use Gaussian similarity with calibrated standard deviations. Graphs used: a six-panel comparison of parameters, a radar chart of the top three sites, a world map with ranked sites, and a summary table.

3) Benefits

The project converts scattered agency datasets into a single, coherent evidence base. It makes analog selection objective and reproducible through documented scoring criteria, supports mission planners in comparing candidate sites, and lowers the entry barrier for students and researchers who lack access to proprietary tools. Because the scripts are modular, users can replace any dataset with their own without rewriting the entire workflow.

4) Intended impact

The intended impact is to accelerate site selection, support equipment testing, and democratize planetary science. By making the search for terrestrial analogs open, transparent, and usable by a wide range of people, the project contributes to the shared knowledge base on which future lunar and Martian missions will depend. As new data become available, the framework can grow with them, extending to new planetary targets and new environmental parameters.

5) Tools, languages, hardware, and software

The project was developed entirely in Python, using Jupyter Notebooks as the primary environment. Key libraries include NumPy and pandas for data handling, Matplotlib for all visualizations, Cartopy for cartographic projections and world maps, global-land-mask for land/ocean filtering, reverse_geocoder for offline place-name resolution, and Requests for NASA POWER API access. The development environment was standard cloud-hosted notebooks (Google Colab) and local Jupyter installations; no specialized hardware was required beyond a standard computer with internet access. The datasets were hosted on NASA servers and required no authentication or paid licenses.

6) Creativity

What makes this project different is how it approaches the problem. Instead of starting from the usual list of NASA training sites, we built a method that scans the whole planet and applies the same transparent criteria to every candidate, so overlooked places can emerge and be compared fairly. This opens the door to unconventional evaluations—looking at a dried sea bed for how it handles dust, or an Andean plateau for ultraviolet exposure, rather than assuming only the classic sites are worth studying. Combining planetary reference data with terrestrial observations gives the analysis a solid physical grounding. At the same time, we were explicit about what cannot be reproduced on Earth, such as Martian gravity or the near-vacuum of the lunar surface, and we flagged those limits in the code and in the outputs. That honesty is part of the design: the tool does not pretend to offer a perfect substitute, but it helps users see clearly which conditions can be tested here and which cannot.

7) Factors considered

Several factors guided the design. First, scientific accuracy: all reference values are tied to published sources, and where data are missing the code documents the gap rather than inventing values. Second, reproducibility: every scoring formula, weight, and threshold is visible in the code. Third, accessibility: the notebooks are written to be understandable by non-specialists, with explanatory comments and readable outputs. Fourth, physical realism: parameters that cannot be reproduced on Earth, such as Martian gravity (0.38 g) and pressure (6 mbar), are explicitly flagged so that no site is mistakenly presented as a complete analog. Finally, scalability: the modular structure allows new parameters, new datasets, and new planetary targets to be added without redesigning the existing workflow.

8) Challenges and limitations

The project faced several constraints worth stating openly. The main one is physical: some reference conditions simply cannot be reproduced on Earth. Martian gravity (0.38 g) and lunar surface pressure (effectively vacuum) are impossible to recreate at scale outside a laboratory, and even the most faithful analog site can only approximate a subset of conditions. A second constraint concerns data coverage: some parameters, such as perchlorate concentration or subsurface thermal diffusivity, are not measured at the same resolution globally, so the composite scores rely on a mix of direct measurements, regional estimates, and literature values. A third limitation is subjectivity in the weights: although every weight is documented and adjustable, the choice of weights inevitably reflects mission priorities, and a different set of priorities would produce a different ranking. Finally, some parameters (biology, operational logistics) were scored qualitatively rather than through continuous data, which introduces additional uncertainty. These limitations do not undermine the tool's usefulness, but they define what it can and cannot claim: it is a decision-support instrument.

9) App design

The E.L.M.A. (Earth-based Lunar & Martian Analogues) web application was designed as a self-contained, single-page, client-side experience built around a modular vanilla JavaScript architecture with no build step, relying on native ES modules and an import map to load Three.js r160 directly from a CDN, while Leaflet 1.9.4 is injected as a classic script for the 2D cartographic layer; the design follows a clear separation between a data layer (a static array of 33 analog sites, each carrying geographic coordinates, a colour code, parameter tables, application tags, source citations, and an eight-dimensional feature vector spanning mineralogy, micro-topography, thermal extremes, cryosphere, aeolian dynamics, subsurface structures, illumination geometry, and extremophile potential), a scoring engine that computes per-planet affinity through a weighted linear combination normalized by the sum of active weights, and a presentation layer composed of three mutually exclusive views (a selection/hero view, an immersive “app mode” with a left-hand site sidebar and right-hand detail panel, and full-screen overlays for the Earth map, the feature-importance editor, and the sources archive). Visually, the interface adopts a dark, cyber-scientific language built on CSS custom properties (cyan, magenta, gold, lime accents over an ink background), glassmorphism panels with backdrop filters, scanline and vignette overlays, and a typographic pairing of Orbitron for technical labels with Space Grotesk for body copy; the 3D scene is rendered by a WebGLRenderer with ACES Filmic tone mapping, an ambient light plus directional “sun” and rim lights, and three textured spheres (Earth, Moon, Mars) whose positions and scales are interpolated toward per-state targets, with procedurally generated canvas fallbacks for all textures in case remote assets fail. Interaction is handled through a Raycaster that resolves pointer events against invisible hit spheres attached to site markers and planetary hotspots, opening a modal with SVG illustrations and quantitative stats, while a floating mascot narrates each site through a typewriter speech bubble. The Earth map was deliberately migrated from a custom equirectangular canvas renderer to a real Leaflet instance, first using CARTO dark tiles and then switching to keyless OpenStreetMap and Esri World Imagery providers to avoid API-key requirements, with markers dynamically filtered by planet and minimum-score sliders and linked bidirectionally to the detail panel. Weight tuning is exposed both in a compact bottom-left panel and in a full feature-importance overlay that renders a canvas radar chart, recalculates all scores on input, and propagates updates to the sidebar, map, and any open detail panel, while the global weight object was kept isolated from local canvas dimensions after a naming collision (a local W shadowing the weights) was identified and fixed. Responsiveness is achieved through CSS media queries that collapse sidebars into half-width columns on mobile and hide non-essential panels, performance is kept acceptable through limited pixel ratio, throttled animations via requestAnimationFrame with a clamped delta, and lazy initialization of the Leaflet map only when the overlay is first opened, and the whole application is bootstrapped by an asynchronous loader that reports texture-fetch progress before revealing the scene, ensuring that the design remains robust, transparent about its data provenance through a dedicated sources panel, and fully functional without any backend or authentication layer.
